extra.message: The login() handler for POST /api/user/login never reads or validates any credentials from req.body — it unconditionally logs the request in as a fixed user ('Jim Bob') and issues an auth token. There is no username/password check whatsoever, so authentication is entirely bypassed; any request to this endpoint succeeds.

cwe: CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function

extra.message: A cryptographically random token is generated with Math.random() but then immediately discarded and replaced with a hardcoded constant string '35592211433686316', which is used as the userAuthToken session identifier for every login. Because the value is static and predictable, any attacker can set this exact cookie value to authenticate as the logged-in user and read/update their profile (see getProfile/updateProfile which trust this cookie as the sole identity check).

cwe: CWE-330: Use of Insufficiently Random Values

extra.message: The userAuthToken session cookie is set without httpOnly, secure, or sameSite attributes. Missing httpOnly allows client-side JavaScript (e.g. via the XSS findings in this codebase) to read the token via document.cookie, and the missing sameSite attribute means the cookie is sent on cross-site requests, enabling CSRF against the endpoints below.

POST /api/user/profile (updateProfile) mutates server-side state keyed only by the userAuthToken cookie, with no CSRF token, Origin/Referer check, or SameSite cookie protection. A malicious page can auto-submit a cross-site POST (the app even ships a dedicated 'csrf' demo view illustrating this exact endpoint) to overwrite a victim's profile, including injecting HTML/script into lastName which is later rendered unsanitized (see the XSS finding in csrf.controller.js).

The session/auth cookie value and full user profile contents are written to server logs via console.log on every profile read/update request, exposing session identifiers and personal data in log files.

cwe: CWE-532: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File

extra.message: The /api/search endpoint echoes req.query.searchTerm back to the client verbatim with no output encoding or sanitization. This raw, attacker-controlled string is the source consumed by the Angular client, which explicitly marks it as trusted HTML (see xss-search.controller.js) and renders it via ng-bind-html, resulting in reflected XSS.

The unsanitized search response from the server (attacker-controlled via the ?searchTerm query parameter, see src/server/routes.js search handler) is explicitly marked as trusted HTML with $sce.trustAsHtml() and stored in vm.searchResults, which is rendered with ng-bind-html="vm.searchResults" in xss-search.html:18. This deliberately bypasses Angular's built-in XSS/SCE protections, producing a reflected XSS sink (e.g. #search-term= in the location hash is fed straight back into search()).

The user profile's lastName field, which is fully attacker-controllable via the unauthenticated/CSRF-vulnerable POST /api/user/profile endpoint (src/server/routes.js updateProfile), is marked as trusted HTML with $sce.trustAsHtml() and rendered via ng-bind-html="vm.user.lastName" in csrf.html:32. Combined with the missing CSRF protection on the profile-update endpoint, an attacker can force a victim's browser to store a malicious lastName (e.g. ) that executes when the victim views their profile — a stored XSS chained from CSRF.

The middleware that would set a Content-Security-Policy header (and could include frame-ancestors) is commented out, and no X-Frame-Options / frameguard middleware is configured anywhere in the app. Responses can therefore be embedded in an attacker-controlled <iframe>, enabling clickjacking attacks (the app even ships a dedicated 'clickjacking' demo view illustrating this).

cwe: CWE-1021: Improper Restriction of Rendered UI Layers (Clickjacking)

extra.message: The session auth token returned from login is additionally stored in sessionStorage, which is directly readable by any JavaScript running in the page context. This widens the impact of the XSS findings in this codebase (an injected script can read sessionStorage and exfiltrate the session token, not just rely on the missing HttpOnly cookie flag).
